output.headline: Europe plans its biggest Russia sanctions package since the war began
output.bodyHtml:
Europe is moving to tighten the pressure on Russia, with the EU poised to approve its biggest sanctions package since the war began and allies including the UK, Germany and Sweden voicing solidarity with Ukraine and concern at the deal, a day after Donald Trump said Ukraine needed “a new leader” and struck a deal to buy Russian diesel from Vladimir Putin, as Russian strikes killed 20 people, including three children, in Ukraine’s south-east.

The diesel deal disrupts four years of western financial pressure on Moscow and leaves Kyiv’s allies in Europe and Nato scrambling to adapt their sanctions plan. The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the diesel deal “provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war”.

“This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t,” she said on Saturday. “On Monday, EU foreign ministers intend to approve the biggest set of sanctions listings targeting Russia’s war machine since the start of the war.” She was referring to plans to formally add 1,600 new individuals and entities to the EU’s sanctions blacklist.

The German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said Berlin “remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions”, adding that support for Ukraine “remains unwavering”.

Ulf Kristersson, the Swedish prime minister, expressed “regret” at the US agreement, saying energy revenues were “a vital source of funding Russia’s war of aggression”.

Andy Burnham reiterated his “complete solidarity” in a call with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the leaders agreed to meet in person in the coming days to continue talks.

The prime minister said he recognised the past day had been “difficult for Ukraine” and the two talked about the importance of keeping up pressure on Russia, No 10 said.

The US president suggested Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war with Russia and blamed him for high diesel prices in the US.

“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Trump said.

Trump made the comments as Russia launched deadly strikes on civilians in Ukraine, which Zelenskyy said were a “thanks” to Trump for the diesel deal.

The Ukrainian president has expressed outrage at the agreement announced by Trump on Friday, which the US president said was needed to reduce diesel prices, and comes ahead of November’s midterm elections in which fuel costs are a key voter issue.

The deal, which appeared to blindside Kyiv as it was announced while Ukrainian negotiators were in Miami for peace talks, was described by Zelenskyy as a “gift” to Russia’s president.

He said Russia would use the money it raised from the fuel sales to invest in its war and that “any easing of sanctions” would play into Russia’s hands, “allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer”.

That prediction was realised hours later, when Ukrainian officials announced that a barrage of Russian strikes on the country’s south-east early on Saturday had killed 20 people, including three children.

“Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said on social media on Saturday.

“Last night confirmed once again that in Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed,” he said.

There were also “large-scale power outages” in the capital, Kyiv, the country’s largest private energy provider said.

In stark contrast to Zelenskyy’s open frustration with Trump, a Kremlin readout of Friday’s call between the US president and Putin was glowing, with the Russian ⁠news agency Interfax ⁠quoting ​an aide as saying it was “very substantive and friendly”.

“Neither wanted to be the first to hang up,” the Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said of the two leaders. “They hung up simultaneously, literally at the same time.” ​Zelenskyy has previously said Putin is playing games with Trump.

Major European governments have attempted to balance their diplomatic and trade relationships with a mercurial Trump and their support for Ukraine.

Related: The more Putin escalates his attacks on Europe, the more Europe should support Ukraine | Timothy Garton Ash

Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia “must feel its losses” and has promised to respond. In the Russian-occupied ‌Luhansk ‌region, Ukrainian attacks in the past 24 hours had killed four ⁠civilians and wounded ⁠five, the region’s ‌Russian-installed governor, Leonid Pasechnik, said ​on Saturday.

Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to take “de-escalatory steps” in the war but only if Russia did the same.

Russia’s fuel production has become a key point of contention between Zelenskyy and Trump, who has attempted to stop Ukraine from bombing Russian refineries, which he says exacerbates a global diesel shortage. The Ukrainian leader has rejected such requests unless Russia stops attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

The Financial Times reported that during the talks in Miami, Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised the possibility that US intelligence sharing could be cut off if Kyiv did not halt the strikes.
output.standfirst: Europe plans its biggest Russia sanctions package since the war began, after Donald Trump struck a diesel deal with Russia, said Ukraine needed a new leader, and Russian strikes killed 20 people, including three children.
output.progress: EU foreign ministers meet on Monday to approve 1,600 new sanctions targets, while Germany reaffirms unwavering support for Ukraine and the UK pledges solidarity.

output.headline: Camden council commissions independent review of nursery safeguarding practice
output.bodyHtml:
After Vincent Chan’s sexual offending came to light, Camden council commissioned an independent local child safeguarding practice review, led by an independent reviewer, to examine how he was able to abuse children at the Finchley Road nursery, in addition to offences committed in his previous role. The review follows a rapid review that Camden council carried out into its decision to clear Chan to return to work after the investigation by Bright Horizons, which concluded in November 2025.

A paedophile nursery worker was cleared by an investigation overseen by a local authority three years before he was arrested.

In February, Vincent Chan was jailed after pleading guilty to 56 offences, including assault by penetration on three-year-old girls in his care at a Bright Horizons nursery on Finchley Road in north-west London. After his conviction, prosecutors described him as a “prolific sexual predator”.

The Guardian can now reveal that Chan was the subject of an earlier safeguarding investigation, carried out by Bright Horizons, with the oversight of Camden council. It followed what were described as “significant concerns” raised with the nursery in 2021 about Chan’s conduct and behaviour by the parent of a young girl, including concerns about what her daughter was saying to her about Chan.

Bright Horizons referred the matter to Camden council, which advised the nursery to investigate. Chan was put on duties that involved no contact with children while the investigation by Bright Horizons took place. After it was completed, Chan was cleared to return to his role caring for young children in the nursery.

A year later, in 2022, Chan filmed himself sexually abusing three-year-old girls at the Bright Horizons nursery.

Nursery staff discovered videos Chan had filmed of distressed children in his care, and he was arrested for the first time in June 2024, initially on suspicion of child cruelty.

When police searched Chan’s devices as part of that investigation, they discovered he was a prolific sexual offender, holding tens of thousands of child abuse images on his computer. He had also committed sexual offences in his previous job as a teaching assistant at St Mary’s Church of England primary school in Dollis Park, north London, including upskirting female pupils. In February this year, Chan was sentenced to 18 years in prison.

The revelation that Camden council and Bright Horizons were aware of concerns about Chan three years before his arrest, and that there had been an investigation into his behaviour, will raise questions about whether there were earlier opportunities to stop him. It will also raise wider questions about whether existing safeguards for nurseries are adequate.

In early 2024, prior to Chan’s arrest, other parents say that they raised concerns with Bright Horizons about Chan’s conduct at work. They say they warned Bright Horizons that their children were telling them that Chan shouted at them, was “angry” and a “bad man”. These parents say these concerns were dismissed. After Chan’s first arrest, the Bright Horizons nursery on Finchley Road closed in June 2025.

Nurseries have a responsibility to refer to local authority designated officers (LADOs) when there are concerns that a nursery worker has been accused of harming or posing a risk of harm to children, may be guilty of criminal conduct, or has exhibited behaviour that makes them unsuitable to work with children.

Local authorities have the ultimate responsibility for managing allegations raised that relate to adults who work with children.

LADOs can recommend that a matter be referred to the police if they believe it meets a criminal threshold. It is understood that the Metropolitan police did not receive a referral in 2021 regarding Chan, and were only notified of the concerns subsequently.

The review, which has been pushed back repeatedly, is expected to be published in early 2027 according to Camden council. It is expected to be critical of the safeguarding culture within Bright Horizons. But Camden council has said publicly that it cannot investigate Bright Horizons under health and safety laws because it is conflicted due to its participation in the safeguarding review. Local authorities have the power to prosecute businesses that do not comply with health and safety legislation.

In a letter to the parent of a child at the nursery, seen by the Guardian, Camden council said that the purpose of the safeguarding review was “not conducted to hold individuals, organisations, or agencies to account”. The review is not expected to satisfy the parents of Chan’s victims because it is unlikely to apportion blame to executives at Bright Horizons.

There has been no explanation of why the review was pushed back from summer 2026, when the independent reviewer was initially expected to submit her report. The council has also rejected a freedom of information request from the Guardian relating to Chan’s employment at the nursery, citing a desire to “manage” the release of information.

It is understood that, in addition to the 2021 referral involving Chan, Camden council received other unrelated safeguarding referrals from Bright Horizons between 2017 and 2024, the time Chan worked at the nursery.

A spokesperson for Camden council said: “Children deserve the best care in a safe environment and the ongoing independent local child safeguarding review into this case presents a pivotal opportunity to prevent abuse like this from happening again. Our participation in the review is thorough, and we have disclosed all relevant documents and information.

“We are ready to receive the review’s recommendations once it is published and take action. We are determined to make a real and tangible impact on safeguarding arrangements for the future.”

A spokesperson for Bright Horizons said: “Our thoughts remain with the victims of Chan’s shocking crimes and their families. As the Camden local authority’s child safeguarding practice review is ongoing, we will not be able to comment without the express written authorisation of that committee as we do not wish to prejudice that process. We will respond as soon as we are able, once we have received the committee’s response.”

• In the UK, the NSPCC offers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text the Childhelp abuse hotline on 800-422-4453. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800; adult survivors can seek help at Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found at Child Helpline International
output.standfirst: The review, delayed repeatedly and due in 2027, follows Vincent Chan’s conviction for 56 offences, after he was cleared of ‘significant concerns’ in 2021 following an investigation by Bright Horizons overseen by Camden council
output.progress: Camden council says it is ready to act on the independent safeguarding review’s recommendations once it is published.

output.headline: Tennessee pauses executions and prison chief resigns over Pike case
output.bodyHtml:
Christa Pike has been discharged from the hospital after surviving Tennessee’s botched 30 September attempt to execute her by lethal injection and is back in prison, her lawyers said on Saturday.

Pike, 50, returned to the Deborah K Johnson rehabilitation center, where she has been imprisoned for the last three decades, her attorneys, Stephen Ferrell, Luke Ihnen, Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason, said in a statement.

“She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances,” Pike’s lawyers added. “She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery.”

Saturday’s update about Pike came 10 days after the death row prisoner was given two doses of pentobarbital, a lethal injection drug, in what proved to be a failed execution attempt. She was hospitalised after surviving the botched execution and was declared brain dead on Monday.

Related: Texas kills man in first US execution since botched lethal injection of Christa Pike

But in a shocking turnaround, on Thursday her lawyer said that she was “up and walking” – though she remained “somewhat foggy” and wasn’t able to use her arms very much.

Pike said that her arms were burning during the failed execution and asked if it was supposed to feel that way. Witnesses present in the chamber said that “nothing was normal” while officials have maintained that they followed every step of Tennessee’s approved execution protocol.

There has been no official explanation about why Pike survived the execution. Medical experts speculate that perhaps some or much of the drug missed her vein and went into surrounding tissue, that one of her veins blew, that the drug was faulty, or a combination of such factors.

Her lawyers months earlier had flagged that Pike’s veins were problematic.

Pike was convicted in 1995 for the torture and murder of Colleen Slemmer, then 18 and her classmate at Knoxville Job Corps. According to court filings, Pike, who was also 19 at the time, was worried Slemmer was trying to take her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, then 17.

Shipp and Pike were convicted of taking Slemmer into a wooded part of the University of Tennessee campus and murdering her. She was given the death penalty, and Shipp was sentenced to life in prison because he was younger than 18.

After Slemmer’s murder, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar and post-traumatic stress disorders, her attorneys said.

“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.”

Pike’s survival of the botched execution has shocked many in the US and overseas and galvanised critics of the death penalty.

Tennessee’s top prison official has announced his resignation.

Meanwhile, the state’s governor, Bill Lee, has paused executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year. And Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, on Friday cancelled a planned lethal injection execution in the state.

But they continue elsewhere.

For instance, the Pentagon confirmed on Thursday that it planned to livestream the execution by firing squad in December of former army psychiatrist Nidal Hassan, who killed 13 people at Texas’s Fort Hood, prompting condemnation from the United Nations.

Donald Trump on Saturday said Hassan “was vicious – he was violent” and that he would “make a decision” about the plans to livestream his execution.

“There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show,” the president remarked. “Because you know by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”
output.standfirst: Tennessee has paused executions and its prison chief has resigned after Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital on 30 September; her lawyers say she remains in the same prison, receiving medical care.
output.progress: Florida's governor, Ron DeSantis, has also cancelled a planned lethal injection execution in the state.

context.text: Tennessee's governor also ordered an independent inquiry into the failed execution, on top of suspending executions and the prison chief's resignation, the Guardian reported.

output.headline: Emergency measures shield up to 130 million from soaring prices, UN says
output.bodyHtml:
Emergency government measures have shielded up to 130 million of the world’s poorest people from the full impact of high prices since the Iran war broke out earlier this year, the report says.

But developing countries still face a triple shock from the energy crisis, El Niño and surging borrowing costs, and need urgent support from the international community, the UN’s development arm has warned.

It warns that many of them are now at risk, as governments run out of the resources needed to keep cushioning their populations against soaring costs.

Speaking before the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok this week, the UNDP’s administrator, Alexander De Croo, called for “solidarity and global action”.

“Developing countries, their hands and legs are being pulled in different directions: it’s truly hard for them,” he said.

Before the meetings, the UNDP published a report, No Time to Recover, which lays out the risks of what it calls the “compounding crises” of energy, climate and debt.

Oil prices have been driven back above $100 a barrel in recent weeks since hostilities resumed in the Middle East.

“What we see now is that countries are pivoting their policy and letting the price hikes flow through. They’re pivoting the policy because they have no choice, because their fiscal space is completely eaten up,” De Croo said.

“We are witnessing a perfect storm that could throw tens if not hundreds of millions of people back into poverty.”

Meanwhile, the worst El Niño climate pattern in perhaps 1,000 years is expected to cause widespread crop failures and increase the risk of extreme weather events, while at the same time the global bond sell-off is driving up government borrowing costs.

De Croo said: “The cost today for bond financing for developing countries, it’s 9 per cent. That is really, really high.”

He added that the situation was expected to deteriorate between now and the spring. “For each of the three things that we mentioned – fuel prices, El Niño and the bond markets – unfortunately for each of those at the moment, we don’t see any light at the end of the tunnel.”

His warning chimes with the findings of separate research published on Sunday by the campaign group Debt Justice, underlining the social impact of high debt servicing costs.

It shows that low-income countries classified by the IMF as either in, or at risk of, debt distress have cut their education budgets by an average of 8 per cent since 2019, and wider public spending by 2 per cent.

Heidi Chow, the executive director of Debt Justice, said: “High levels of debt are having a devastating impact on people’s access to healthcare and education.”

Debt Justice is calling for the outright cancellation of some of the most burdensome debts, and overhaul of the IMF-administered common framework for debt restructuring.

Chow said: “We urgently need debt cancellation – especially from the highest interest lenders like banks, hedge funds and oil traders.”

De Croo said the UNDP did not oppose efforts to secure debt relief for some of the hardest-hit countries – but argued it would take many months to negotiate, and instead called for more urgent action.

“We urge the international community – multilateral lenders, donors, and partners – to step up access to affordable finance so countries can sustain support for their most vulnerable households,” De Croo said.

He praised the IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva’s recent call for spending restraint in developed countries, in the hope of taming bond yields.

But he said: “We also need to have a coordinated policy for developing countries. And that coordinated policy for developing countries cannot just be, ‘you are at the end of the line and we’ll see what happens’.”

He declined to say what the specific response should be, but stressed that it should create “time and space” for developing countries to carry out much-needed changes.

During the Covid crisis, G20 nations implemented a temporary standstill on debt repayments for developing countries.

De Croo also pointed to liquidity measures available to central banks, such as the currency swap lines implemented by the US Federal Reserve during recent financial crises, to prevent markets seizing up. “What would help is a certain level of liquidity,” he said.
output.standfirst: Emergency measures have shielded up to 130 million people from high prices, but the UN warns fiscal space has run out, risking a perfect storm that could push tens or hundreds of millions into poverty.
output.progress: The UNDP is urging multilateral lenders and donors to widen access to affordable finance for the most vulnerable developing countries.

output.headline: Man dies after jumping into tiger enclosure at Yorkshire zoo
output.bodyHtml:
A man has died after being attacked by a tiger after jumping into its enclosure at a zoo in Yorkshire, police have said.

Emergency services were contacted shortly after 1.30pm on Saturday when the man entered the enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, near Doncaster, and was set upon by the tiger.

He was pronounced dead at the scene, South Yorkshire police said, adding his family had been informed.

Videos circulating online appear to show a man being pawed at and grappled by a tiger in an enclosure.

A police spokesperson said the tiger attacked the man and inflicted “serious injury”.

“Emergency services attended and sadly, despite the best efforts of medical personnel, the man was pronounced dead at the scene,” they added.

“Regarding rumours surrounding the condition of the tiger, the animal was uninjured and remained in the enclosure following the incident and there is no wider risk to the public.”

The force urged people not to share “distressing” video footage of the attack, circulating on social media.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park said a “serious incident” occurred inside the enclosure.

It said in a statement: “Our emergency response procedures were immediately activated, and emergency services are currently attending the scene.

“We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened.” It added that the “safety and wellbeing of visitors, staff and animals remain our highest priority”.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park opened in 2009, with the Land of the Tigers attraction opening in 2011.

The attraction is on a purpose-built two-acre reserve for Amur tigers, an endangered subspecies with about 500 left in the wild.

Photos of the enclosure on the park’s website shows a high walkway for visitors and fencing above the section where the tigers can roam.

A Yorkshire ambulance service spokesperson said it sent a number of resources to the scene including two ambulances, Yorkshire air ambulance and a doctor.
output.standfirst: Police said there is no wider risk to the public after a man died on Saturday when he was attacked by a tiger after entering its enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park.
output.progress: South Yorkshire police confirmed no wider risk to the public, and ambulance crews, an air ambulance and a doctor were sent to the scene.

output.headline: Government-allied forces claim recapture of Bab al-Mandab strait from Houthis
output.bodyHtml:
Forces allied to Yemen’s UN-recognised government claim to have mounted a successful offensive to retake the Bab al-Mandab strait from Houthi rebels, though accounts vary as to whether the push has in fact been repelled. The claim came as the latest Houthi missile attack on the international airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh, killed 12 people and injured more than 300 others, an attack a Saudi-led coalition blamed on Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen.

A Houthi spokesperson said forces from the Saudi-backed government based in Aden “were targeted with a large number of ballistic missiles, artillery support and heavy weapons, resulting in the destruction of more than 22 armoured vehicles and the killing and wounding of dozens, including a number of commanders.

“More than 30 ambulances arrived in Aden to transport the dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations.”

By contrast, the Saudi ambassador to Yemen, Mohammed al-Jaber, said: “Blessed Friday and victory for every Yemeni and Arab. Bab al-Mandab has been cleared of the remnants of the Houthi terrorist militia.”

The exposed 5 sq mile (13 sq km) Perim Island straddles the strait, acting as a lookout point for all traffic from the Red Sea into the Gulf of Aden and towards the Indian Ocean. Aidarous al-Zubaidi, the president of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), one of the main political forces in the south of Yemen, claimed the island and coastal area had been recaptured from Houthi hands.

An official military spokesperson for the UN-recognised government forces qualified the claim, saying only half the area had been recaptured so far. Waddah al-Dabish said newly established Houthi defensive lines had been broken on the land next to the strait, leading to the death of thousands of Houthi fighters.

It is thought that as many as 500 Houthi fighters are stationed on the island, and Saudi Arabia is desperate to be able to report that the strait has been reclaimed to show that the land counteroffensive it launched at the beginning of the week is advancing.

The report came as the United Nations’ special envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, admitted to the UN security council in New York that Yemen – one of the poorest countries in the world – had lapsed back into full-scale war and said the first victims would be women and children.

The Houthis seized control of the strait two weeks ago and said no Saudi-linked commercial traffic would be permitted to go through the narrow waterway. The Houthis are waging a war to remove Saudi influence from Yemen, and have been mounting missile attacks on Riyadh in support of this objective.

There have been previous premature reports of military breakthroughs by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government since it launched its counteroffensive at the start of the week, but the recapture of the land by the strait and Perim Island (also known as Mayyun Island) is a military prize western governments desperately need.

The US president, Donald Trump, said he was evaluating whether the US should join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen. “We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump said. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”

The US secretary of ⁠state, Marco ⁠Rubio, called the attacks “​reprehensible” and said “they must ​stop ‌now”.

The latest attack on the international airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital of Riyadh killed 12 people and injured more than 300 others, civil aviation authorities said early Sunday, with some in a critical condition. A Saudi-led coalition blamed Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen.

A missile struck a King Khalid international airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorised to speak to the media.

A Saudi statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said the injured were being treated at several hospitals.

One witness at the Riyadh airport reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded.

“I was on gate 403,” at the domestic terminal, the witness told the Agence France-Presse news agency. “I saw [gate] 401 hit, I saw injured [people] in front of my eyes. Everyone was running.”

The relative of one injured person said they had been wounded in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass and taken to hospital.

Related: Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?

A projectile also fell near the King Fahd international airport in Dammam, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis. The Dammam airport has become an important alternative to Riyadh amid the recent spate of attacks.

There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sana’a international airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.

Saturday’s incident comes amid an escalation of missile strikes by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis ⁠on the kingdom. The airport has already been attacked twice this ​week, leaving four people dead and ‌others wounded, and ‌badly damaging an aircraft.

The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.
output.standfirst: Government-allied forces say they have broken Houthi defensive lines and retaken about half of the Bab al-Mandab strait, as a missile strike on Riyadh airport blamed on Houthi rebels killed 12 people and injured more than 300.
output.progress: The injured are being treated at several hospitals, while the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, has demanded the strikes stop immediately.

context.text: A Saudi-led coalition said a 100-jet air campaign had secured ‘air protection’ of the Bab al-Mandab strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets.

output.headline: 250,000 march through London in solidarity with Palestinians, organisers say
output.bodyHtml:
Thousands of people have gathered in central London to express their support for Palestinians, marking three years since Israel began what many call a ‘genocide’ against them.

Husam Zomlot, the Palestinian ambassador to the UK, shared a video from the march on social media, saying: ‘Three years on, Israel’s atrocities in Gaza and the West Bank continue, and so does the solidarity of the British people. Louder, bigger and not going anywhere. Thank you all.’ Organisers said 250,000 people joined the march by Saturday afternoon.

The national march is the first held since the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements and declared the UK government would take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety. He also told the Commons that settler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank.

At Labour party conference last month, Miliband appeared to reference the marches, which at their peak regularly numbered hundreds and thousands of people, telling the audience in Liverpool: ‘I want to say to the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you, you were right.’

The demonstrators, many wearing keffiyehs and holding Palestine flags, gathered on the Embankment at midday on Saturday. A bride and groom appeared to be among those in attendance, and a two-minute silence was held to reflect on the lives lost in Gaza. Some carried placards reading ‘End the genocide’ and ‘Free Palestine’ as they marched towards parliament.

The Metropolitan police said 20 arrests had been made, including for criminal damage after demonstrators climbed on to the Battle of Britain memorial, held Palestine Action placards, made a Nazi salute and assaulted police as officers made arrests.

Protesters were calling for the UK government to stop supplying arms to Israel, which various bodies – including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based – have said is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

A ceasefire was declared a year ago but Israeli airstrikes have continued in Gaza. In the last year, the overall death toll has risen by a further 1,400 people. Settlers have also ramped up their attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank. According to UN figures, 230 Palestinians were killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces and settlers in 2025.

Related: ‘Neither war nor peace’: Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruins

The Met have imposed conditions on the event – which is organised by the Palestine Coalition, which has organised more than 30 mass demonstrations since October 2023, with a counter-protest by Stop The Hate – to ‘minimise the risk of serious disruption to communities’.

The Met posted on X saying: “The front of the procession has now entered Whitehall where a rally will take place.

“Several arrests have been made so far including a woman and a man with placards declaring support for proscribed organisation Palestine Action.

“We have also arrested a number of protesters on suspicion of criminal damage after they climbed on to the Battle of Britain memorial on Victoria Embankment.”

Deputy assistant commissioner Carl Galvin said: ‘We know Saturday’s event, so close to the third anniversary of the terror attack on Israel, has the potential to have a greater impact on communities than the previous national marches.’

Galvin, who is leading the policing operation this weekend, said the force’s presence on Saturday will be ‘significant’.

‘We will also be using powers under the Public Order Act requiring anyone in the protest area wearing face coverings to deliberately conceal their identity to remove them,’ Galvin continued.

The Met have imposed conditions on the march and require the group to travel via Westminster Bridge, York Road, Waterloo Bridge and The Strand on to Whitehall, with a rally concluding by 6.30pm. The force has said that any speeches and music must conclude by 5.30pm.

Related: British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed Miliband

A counter-protest by Stop The Hate is also taking place, with about 30 people gathered outside New Scotland Yard, some with flags.

The force has also imposed conditions on the demonstration ‘to minimise the risk of serious disruption’. The demonstrators must remain within a designated area outside the Met’s headquarters, with the assembly concluding at 2.30pm.

Last Saturday, on the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks, when Hamas militants broke across the Israeli border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals, killing at least 1,209 people, a small pro-Palestine student demonstration in central London was held.

The Met publicly appealed to those behind the demonstration to ‘exercise [their] right to protest on a different date’ and admitted that finding the organisers had been ‘frankly difficult’. In the end, it went ahead and about 100 people attended. Five people were arrested for breaching conditions imposed on the march.

The Palestine Coalition organising the march includes Palestine Solidarity Campaign, Stop the War, CND, the Muslim Association of Britain, Friends of Al Aqsa and the Palestinian Forum in Britain.
output.standfirst: Hundreds of thousands marched through London – the first protest since the UK declared Israel’s occupation of the West Bank unlawful – as police arrested 20 people three years into what marchers call a ‘genocide’.

output.headline: Northern lights dazzle the UK, with more auroras to come
output.bodyHtml:
The northern lights lit up skies across the UK on Friday and Saturday evening.

Sky-gazers as far south as Devon, Hampshire and Kent were treated to the dazzling aurora borealis, also known as the northern lights.

The Met Office said clear skies could bring further sightings until Tuesday.

The display is usually visible only near the Arctic Circle and northern Scotland.

The aurora borealis is a natural light display in Earth’s sky, produced when solar activity and geomagnetic storms interact with the upper atmosphere.

The Met Office said sightings would remain possible until Tuesday across Scotland and similar geomagnetic longitudes, during clear skies.

These displays occur when charged particles collide with gases in the Earth’s atmosphere around the magnetic poles. As they collide, light is released at various wavelengths, creating colourful patterns in the sky.

The Met Office said the sun constantly sends out charged particles known as solar wind, which travel at about 1m mph.

Related: Intense geomagnetic storms could make auroras visible in southern US

The forecaster said: “When these particles interact with Earth’s magnetic field – especially when the solar wind’s polarity is opposite to Earth’s – they are funnelled toward the magnetic poles.

“As these energetic particles collide with gases in the upper atmosphere, they release energy in the form of light. Oxygen produces green and, at higher altitudes, rare red auroras, while nitrogen creates blue and purple hues.”

Last year, experts said 2026 would be a peak year for aurora-spotting, as the sun has been in a heightened state of activity as part of its 11-year natural cycle.
output.standfirst: Though usually confined to the far north, the aurora borealis dazzled sky-gazers as far south as Devon, Hampshire and Kent, with the Met Office saying clear skies could bring further sightings until Tuesday.
output.progress: The Met Office is tracking the solar activity and says clear skies could bring further sightings across the UK until Tuesday.
